title: Context strip
summary: Adds P16 Context strip (draft): when an engine's controls pick part of a bigger fixed whole (multisample zones, wavetable frames, a built-in recording) and the drawing is a close-up, a small detail-callout map of the whole sits under the header; plus the narrow craft.md exception.
rationale: Asked for by the guidelines' owner on 2026-11-04: engines can carry a top strip with grid context, such as where on a keyboard a multisample engine is, or where on a sample or waveform. Grounded in open-xy staging 6b2d113: the display Input has note activity but no pitch, a sampler-based engine plays one sample chromatically from a root key, and the sample overview is 96 bins whose begin/end markers follow every edit including stockShift trims. No screen has used it yet, so it's marked a draft pattern.

changes.content:
## P16 · Context strip

**The idea.** A draft pattern: no audited screen uses it yet; the mock in its proposal (`training/proposals/2026-11-04-context-strip/mock-rest.png`) shows the intent. Some engines play from something bigger than one picture: a multisample synth's zones across the keyboard, a wavetable's frames, a recording built into the engine. When the controls pick part of that whole and the drawing is a close-up of the part, I put a small map of the whole right under the header, drawn the way a technical drawing marks a detail: a ruler of the whole, an outlined bracket on the part the controls pick, and two faint callout lines down to corner marks around the close-up. The drawing stays the picture every control changes; the map only answers "which part of the whole is this?". It's the top-edge partner to P5's activity strip: that one says what's happening, this one says where you are.

**Why it works.** A close-up loses its frame of reference. With one wavetable frame drawn large, the player can't tell how far through the table it is; with one zone drawn large, they can't tell which octave it covers. A detail callout is how drawings have always answered that, so it reads as part of the drawing rather than an interface: no scroll bar, no filled value bar echoing the header, no text.

**When it's there.** Only when both hold: the controls select part of a whole that the drawing doesn't show, and I can say in one sentence what the map tells the player that the drawing doesn't. Then it's part of the resting page, as `craft.md` allows. Otherwise there's no strip, not even while a control turns. A sample engine never gets one: its drawing is the sample's overview, which already is the whole (`categories.md`), and a strip would draw it twice. If a control's only picture is a keyboard (a scale, a kit's spacing), that's P13's corner keyboard, not this.

**Build it.**

- **Drawn in the screen's language.** The ruler, bracket and callout belong to the drawing's own language (`craft.md`, One drawing language): an atlas gets a locator inset, a patent section gets a detail callout.
- **Where and how big.** Below y 20 under the stock header, below y 38 under the two-page header (`tokens.json` → `header`). My starting values are a 2 px gap and about 10–12 px of height, slimmer than P5's 16 px bottom strip (`body.stripTop`–`stripBottom`). It spans the drawing's width, not the screen's, which keeps it from reading as a second header row under the stepped bar.
- **The ruler is static artwork.** The whole is the engine's own fixed data (its zone map, its table, its recording), so the ruler is authored once and never redraws. All 128 MIDI notes across 480 px is 3.75 px a key, so a keyboard ruler marks octaves (a tick per C, 45 px apart) or only the range the engine maps (four octaves is 10 px a key). A wavetable ruler is one tick per frame, sized by that frame's brightness, kept ≥ 3 px apart.
- **The bracket is two nodes.** An outlined window (left and right edges, or one outline when its width is fixed), driven by the controls through `Input` the way every other part is, easing 0.15–0.2 s. Turning it costs two nodes; at rest it costs nothing.
- **Weights and greys.** The ruler and its ticks are hairlines (1–1.2 px) in `#646464`, guides in the `craft.md` weights table. The bracket is the meaningful mark, so it's a line weight (1.5 px) in `#AFAFAF` and at least 3 px across. Callout lines are hairline decoration in `#4B4B4B`; corner marks are `#646464`. The brightest thing on screen stays in the drawing.

**Pitfalls.**

- **Possible isn't the bar.** open-xy says what the device can draw; the OP-XY's own look decides what belongs on the page. A map that's buildable but busy, bright, filled or labelled fails here even if it lints clean.
- **The screen doesn't know which key was played.** The display input has note activity but no pitch (`draw.hpp`, `Input`), so a keyboard map shows the range the controls select, never the key under the player's finger. If a note shows on the map at all, the bracket lifts 2 px and brightens one grey step and eases back: decoration on top of the drawing's own note response, not the note response itself, paced like P13 (at most one every ~0.34 s).
- **Context, not a control's channel.** The bracket sliding along the ruler clears the 24 px position floor but changes too little of the screen to pass a control's perceptibility alone; the control still has to move the drawing.
- **Don't repeat the header.** The header shows the value in real units; the map shows where it sits.
- **One strip at rest.** Header, map, drawing and P5's bottom strip make four bands, which is a panel. With a context map, a bottom strip only shows while its own control is in use.
- **Leaving draft.** The server never draws a discipline into a design pass, so I try it on purpose, as the focus of a frames pass. It stops being a draft when an audited library screen uses it and its card says what the map added.

Revision 3. Narrowed to engines whose controls pick part of a bigger fixed whole (multisample zones, wavetable frames, a built-in recording): the ruler is static artwork and the bracket two nodes, which removes the scaled outlines, the seam, stroke scaling, the 32-node peak, the marker-source question and the stockShift dependency (audit 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8). Sample engines get no strip, since their drawing already is the whole (review 5). craft.md exception narrowed to rest-only with the one-sentence test, and the turn-only case dropped (both 2/1). Drawn as a detail callout in the screen's language, spanning the drawing's width, outlined bracket, no filled bar (review 2). At most one strip at rest (review 3). Cell fallback dropped (review 4). Flare defined: 2 px and one step, decoration on top, paced (audit 9, review 6). Bracket at line weight and >= 3 px; hairlines only for the ruler (audit 5). Lint-clean mock rest frame added beside the proposal (review 7).

findings: 1. Narrow the craft.md exception and make it match P16. As written, 'otherwise it shows while its control turns and settles away' reads as permission to show a strip during turns on any page. It contradicts P16's rule of no strip when the drawing already shows the whole, and P16's 'In between' case is never defined. Rewrite craft.md so the strip stays at rest only when the controls select part of a whole the drawing doesn't show, and when it passes P16's one-sentence test (name the test in craft.md). Drop the general 'otherwise' clause, or replace it with the one defined case, with an example.

2. Item 0: present it as a drawing convention, not an interface element. Replace the scroll-bar analogy with one from the drawing languages: an atlas locator inset, a detail callout on a technical drawing, a ruler with a bracket. Say the strip is drawn in the screen's named drawing language (craft.md, One drawing language). Make the selection an outlined bracket or hairline window, not a filled bar that echoes the header's value bars. Say it must not be mistaken for a second header row. Let its width follow the drawing instead of requiring full width.

3. Don't allow both strips at rest. Header, top strip, drawing and P5's bottom strip make four bands, and that is a panel, especially under the 38 px two-page header. Say at most one strip on the resting page. If both are earned, the second one only appears while its control turns.

4. Drop the 32-cell fallback for the sample strip, or redraw it. Three greys of cells put sample level on shade alone (accessibility.md, Meaning never rides on one cue), and a full-width row of cells is exactly the 'strips of cells' craft.md keeps off the resting page. If a fallback is needed, show level by cell height in one grey, or fall back to one outline.

5. Finish removing the zoom premise for samplers. A sampler only has the 96-bin overview, and categories.md makes the overview its subject. So either name a sampler drawing that really is a close-up without being a magnified overview (for example a slice stack or grain field for the region between the markers) and use it as the sampler example in 'Why it works', or limit P16 to engines and remove sampler from catalog.json and the categories row.

6. Say what 'lifts the selected zone a step' means: one grey step, a step taller, or both. If it's a shade step, say it's the second cue after the drawing's own note response, so that a note on the strip never rests on shade alone.

7. Before approval, show the owner one lint-clean mock rest frame at 1:1, outside the proposal since frames can't be part of a training change. Item 0 can't be settled from prose; neither I nor any later reviewer has seen a context strip under the stock header.
